items.summary: When Metal Gear Solid 2 launched 25 years ago it seemed almost indecipherable. Today, it's clear that Kojima's

content.v: https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/11/13/mgs2-retrospective-1794582279618.jpg
This is an IGN opinion piece from Carlos Morales. He’s a long-time fan of the Metal Gear franchise and is an advocate for video games as an artform.

Metal Gear Solid may not be the biggest franchise nowadays, but it was one of the pillars of the first three PlayStation console generations. The adventures of the legendary Solid Snake and his counterparts were not just some of the most critically acclaimed and financially successful games on their respective platforms – they also stand as fantastic and emotional works of art. And what a game Metal Gear Solid 2: Sons of Liberty is, marking its 25th anniversary this year as somehow having become only more relevant and timely now than it was upon its original release on November 13th, 2001.

Series creator Hideo Kojima may have since moved on to new IPs like Death Stranding and his upcoming espionage action game Physint, but the iconic game director’s narrative idiosyncrasies and uncanny ability to predict how society will develop have rarely felt as fully formed as they do in Metal Gear Solid’s first PlayStation 2 entry. Let’s take a look at why MGS2 was so ahead of its time.
Raiden High

To understand MGS2’s place in contemporary culture, we first have to look at it in a historical context. It may be hard to remember now after so many years of reappraisal, but MGS2 proved somewhat divisive on its initial release. The game received excellent reviews and sold more than seven million copies , but it also attracted controversy for its choice of protagonist and its convoluted storyline. Many fans were upset that most of the game was spent playing as new hero Raiden instead of Snake, and that the game was full of long cutscenes and Codec calls where characters spoke at length about philosophical and sociological issues. In a world that was still getting used to constant internet access becoming more prevalent and was uncertain about what social changes the digital age would bring, MGS2 was a complex game that many in the gaming space, both consumer and professional, didn’t know how to process.
https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/11/13/mgs2-raiden-1794581693836.jpg

Even IGN’s Ed Lewis said as much in his review of Metal Gear Solid 3: Snake Eater back in 2004, writing that MGS2’s story was of little interest “unless you really want to spend a couple of late, smoky nights going over the details and putting all the pieces together, and they do fit together. While that's kind of interesting if you want a pleasant mind rutting, it was far from fun to watch a game eat itself.”

But time has been kind to MGS2, because many of the topics Kojima explored in the game would become more relevant in the years that followed. The ways social media, the proliferation of digital misinformation for political purposes, and the normalization of automated warfare, deep fakes, and generative AI would turn rifts between demographics into chasms and create a society where many have a tenuous grasp on what reality even is , were all predicted years in advance by Kojima’s landmark title.

MGS2 is a dense text, and such works can need time to digest. Raiden may have irritated some players in 2001, but he’s now generally accepted as a worthwhile protagonist in his own right by series fans, although it probably doesn’t hurt that Metal Gear Solid 4 turned him into a badass cyborg ninja. People interested in video games as an artform have often pointed to MGS2’s thematic depth , with the game’s story exploring ideas like social engineering, digital censorship, cyberwarfare, and post-truth society. If you just want a tactical espionage adventure with big twists, stealth gameplay, and epic boss fights, the game delivers on those expectations. Yet players embracing MGS2’s more cerebral attributes has made the game an enduring phenomenon even a quarter century later.
One attribute in particular, its metatextual use of game design elements as part of its storytelling, is a big part of why it’s such an impressive artistic achievement.
Game Plays You

MGS2 opens with a prologue featuring series protagonist Solid Snake infiltrating a tanker in the Hudson River to gather evidence of a new Metal Gear prototype named Ray. His ill-fated mission results in the ship sinking, Metal Gear Ray being stolen by recurring villain Revolver Ocelot, and Snake assumed dead. Fast forward two years to a facility called the Big Shell having been built where the tanker sank, which has been taken over by terrorists called Dead Cell and an army of Russian mercenaries under the command of Solidus Snake, one of Snake’s evil clones. They have the President hostage and are seeking to launch a nuclear strike. Raiden, a new agent of FOXHOUND (the same outfit Snake used to work for), is ordered to rescue the hostages and stop the terrorists. Sounds like a standard setup, but it’s not too long into Raiden’s mission that it becomes obvious something is amiss.

Raiden’s mission to the Big Shell has numerous parallels to Snake’s infiltration of Shadow Moses in Metal Gear Solid 1, with repeated plot events, scripted sequences, and character appearances. As the game goes on, the player learns that the entire incident has been orchestrated by a shadow group known as the Patriots, who have covertly controlled the United States government for decades. They’ve also controlled Raiden’s life for years, with his girlfriend Rosemary (who also saves the game for you) being a Patriot agent. The allusions to Shadow Moses are intentional, part of an artificial intelligence simulation system designed to control human behavior and generate desired outcomes. Kojima explicitly makes this plot twist a metaphor for how video game players are conditioned to perform certain actions by subconsciously responding to design choices, with most linear, narrative driven games like the MGS series giving players little to no choice but to do exactly what the developers intend.

Kojima’s metatextual take on the mechanics of game design predates similar attempts to tie player agency (or lack thereof) into the storytelling of games like BioShock or Spec Ops: The Line. Later levels draw attention to simulational and constructed aspects of video game structure, such as the reveal that the Colonel who Raiden has been taking orders from all game long is one of the Patriots’ AIs, or a big fight on an elevator trying to trick players with a fake Mission Failed screen. Even the environments themselves become less “real” inside the cavernous halls of Arsenal Gear, the flying fortress the terrorists seek to use. The levels have a similar design and color scheme to the VR training missions from the first game, and the room where Raiden battles a fleet of Metal Gear Rays is a surreal space that seems to go on for eternity.

These and other parts of Metal Gear Solid 2 are as interesting to experience now as they were on release. Yet the area where the game is most relevant in 2026 is how it reflects the distorted reality of the mid-2020s.
He Tried To Tell Us

It’s strange to play a video game from 2001 and see it predict the last decade of social upheaval. The gears of late-stage capitalism in the digital age have seen information control and cultural mythology become the most important weapons of the ruling class. In much the same way that the Patriots seek to restrict the free flow of information using the AI system known as GW, so too have the real world military industrial complex and ruling government bodies weaponized social media, digital news distribution, and automated misinformation infrastructure to make it harder to tell what is real or not to suit the interests of the powers that be. The rise of generative AI has done untold damage to the social contract and our ability to believe literally anything we see online, which is not a great development in a world where not using the internet is no longer really an option.

items.summary: Just a couple days after Blizzard changed the way gold was earned in max-level quests WoW Forever, the company

content.v: https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/09/19/forever-1789805930640.png

Just a couple days after Blizzard changed the way gold was earned in max-level quests WoW Forever, the company has implemented a weekly quest with loot-box-style gold reward. And players don't love it .

Max level players have found a quest in Booty Bay called 'In Demand - Ancient Elven Curiosities,' which is offered each week, according to Wowhead . There is potential that the quest will rotate to different high level dungeons, but so far, for the two weeks Forever has been out, it's pointed players at Dire Maul, where they have to collect three items. The quest rewards a little bag that can drop one of four items at random that are worth either 10g, 20g, 40g, or 100g.

But while this is a way to get gold in a game where money is scarce, it is rubbing a lot of players in the community the wrong way. For a lot of people, it reminds them of retail WoW, which is built on top of piles and piles of weekly quests to pump additional gold into the economy.

WoW YouTuber Bellular posted the Wowhead link on X / Twitter, captioned simply by "uh what," and followed that up with some criticisms of the new weekly quest. He said: "Retail slop, kill! The way to generate gold is crafting, gathering, selling items. Want to do UBI? Make it sneaky via those means. Don’t show the hand of the designer so clearly." Bellular then tagged Blizzard associate production director Clayton Stone and added: "(pardon the spicy language - some genuine feedback) Let the player earn organically through game systems, not by making content a hoop to jump through."

But it's not just Bellular who's upset at the weekly quest. It's a similar sentiment over on Reddit, where ThatOldGuy7863 simply said : "dear god not weeklys." Meanwhile, drtakhs added: "F**k weeklies and dailies. I’ve been pretty happy with all the decision so far and the thought process behind them was reasonable. Now, what is this? Who wants this? No dailies, no weeklies and no FOMO bulls**t are among the most important things that make classic feel… well like classic…"
However, there may be an explanation for Blizzard's move here. EvadableMoxie suggested a repeatable quest for 100 gold "is aggressively anti-bot."

"It reduces the biggest benefit that bots have, the ability to run 24/7 by frontloading gold rewards," the continued. "This of course does not make bots useless but it reduces their advantage while letting players focus on other things than grinding out gold."

Blizzard has long struggled with bots messing with the economy in every version of World of Warcraft. In the beta, the company had to come down hard on people who were buying and selling gold, which is a direct consequence of botting. Simply put, it's not hard to program a bot to crawl zones for you and gather mining, herbalism or other materials to sell en masse on the auction house. A weekly quest that rewards gold could help players that don't have the time to compete with bots dumping industrial amounts of crafting materials keep up.

But players aren't mad that Blizzard is adding a way to earn gold. Rather, it's the addition of a weekly quest, that encourages players to log on every single week for fear of missing out on an injection of gold. This sort of repeatable quest also wasn't in the original game, with most types of daily and weekly quests not being added until The Burning Crusade.

This is just the latest change as Blizzard tries to nail down the identity of WoW Forever. While there are some parts of the original game that the company has stood firm on, like group tagging , there is an ever growing list of gameplay systems that Blizzard is actively tweaking in Forever, like Dungeon Experience and now, gold rewards.

items.title: 专家表示，GTA 6 和其他游戏的 80 美元价格是合理的
items.summary: Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 finally releases on November 19, and you'll have to pay at least $80 for it. Tha

content.v: Rockstar's Grand Theft Auto 6 finally releases on November 19, and you'll have to pay at least $80 for it. That's a full $20 more than what GTA 5 cost in 2013 and $10 more than many other big AAA games today. Is $80 going to become the "new normal" for AAA games, or is it, along with Nintendo's Mario Kart World and Tears of the Kingdom for Switch 2 , an outlier at $80?

According to Alinea Analytics researcher Rhys Elliott , $80 won't be an across-the-board new price for all games. Some developers will purposefully price their games lower to draw in more consumers--he pointed to games like Expedition 33 ($50), Phantom Blade Zero ($60), and Oblivion Remastered ($50) as examples.
https://www.gamespot.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/Ambrosia_06_a679c3.jpg?w=636

Elliott said that when GTA 6 inevitably becomes a huge success with its $80 and $100 editions, some publishers will be "jumping for joy" because they'll take this as a signal that the market will indeed accept these higher prices.

However, Elliott said he hopes the industry doesn't learn the wrong lessons from GTA 6 and its $80 price point. "GTA 6 is as inelastic as things get in entertainment. People will pay anything to get their mitts on this one, which makes it seem like the perfect Trojan horse for an industry-wide price rise," he said.

"The $80 price point will be a Godsend to some publishers, but it’ll be a snowball's chance in hell for others. After all, this kind of stuff can be zero-sum. When a player spends $100 on GTA 6, their remaining budget shrinks," he added.

Elliott went on to list off some of the studios and game franchises that could likely get their fanbases to buy in at $80. He said these include the next big God of War game after Laufey, the next Naughty Dog game, Intergalactic: The Heretic Prophet, and future Forza titles (assuming Xbox strips them out of Game Pass). Additionally, Elliott said From Software "has the cache" to charge $80 for its new games, while Hogwarts Legacy 2 could also up the price to $80. Elliott added that some of the top sports games could charge more, but that might be a tougher sell considering those games are full of microtransactions already.
"So not all games were created equal, and mid-tier AAA publishers--and also bigger publishers offering smaller games or remakes--will price downward at $40-$60," Elliott said.

There are a lot of factors at play here. For starters, GTA 5 launched at $60 back in 2013, and that same $60 is worth $86 today after inflation, making GTA 6--at least its $80 edition--effectively cheaper than GTA 5 .

At the same time, many people are acutely aware that their pay has not kept up with inflation, while the federal minimum wage hasn't moved up since 2009. GTA 6 is also coming out at a rough time for many people, with gas and grocery prices surging , and the cost of everyday goods generally spiking due in part to increasing inflation. And anyone heading to a store to buy a console to play GTA 6 on is in for some serious sticker shock, as game consoles today are more expensive than ever due to the AI craze.

New video games generally staying the same price over the years has had serious negative effects on the entire industry, experts have said. It's part of the reason why publishers now try to squeeze people more with DLC, battle passes, microtransactions, collector's editions, paid early access, and more. Recently, an Xbox advertising chief said price increases would be a hard sell, so the company is turning to ads to help offset ballooning budgets and keep the business healthy.

items.title: “第 10 季对我们来说是一个具有挑战性的赛季”：在收到偏袒投诉后，Marvel Rivals 正在升级 Storm 的夏季皮肤
items.summary: Storm's reworked legendary skin will be here for Christmas.

content.v: Skin distribution seems to be an issue in pretty much any game with more than one hero and clear favourites. Marvel Rivals has come under fire for it for a while now, ever since players got wise to which heroes were favourites and which had clearly been shoved to the side.

It all came to a head a few months ago when the summer skins were released, and it was revealed that Storm was the only female hero to not get a legendary costume among all the swimsuit designs. Players did not look upon this favourably , as Storm is a hugely popular character and had already gone a long time without the same kind of legendary skins as other heroes like Luna Snow and had been passed over for skins in the Disco and Egyptian God skin lines.
https://cdn.mos.cms.futurecdn.net/cignQhCHEH2w3ijWjM9BmY-1920-80.jpg

But all the player complaints seem to have gotten through to NetEase, with creative director Guangyun Chen acknowledging in a dev diary that "season 10 has been a challenging one for us." Not only were players upset about only one hero being released this season, but the devs have "been closely following the community's feedback regarding certain heroes receiving fewer costumes. With strong demands for more high-quality Legendary costumes featuring recolours and ultimate ability visual upgrades."

The decision has since been made to upgrade Storm's summer skin to legendary tier with the devs "targeting a release around Christmas this December" for it. Other slightly forgotten heroes who will be getting some visual upgrades include Human Torch, who will get a legendary costume in early December which includes "recolours and ultimate ability VFX". Cloak and Dagger will also be getting a (presumably Valentines Day-themed) skin in February.

"We've been hard at work at this for almost eight months," Guangyun Chen says. "Cloak's design will include full legs. We fully re-animated Cloak's entire movement set strictly for this, we really hope you enjoy it."

But with all these new redesigns and costumes on the way, Guangyun Chen wants to remind players that skins can't just be made or changed at a moment's notice: "Please understand that art asset production requires a certain lead time and simply can't be done overnight. Generally, a single costume takes eight to 10 months to produce from start to finish."

Storm's redesigned summer skin has been in the works for three months already, with the finished product coming out after five months of work. That's under the average of eight to 10 months, but this sounds like the exception not the rule.

items.title: 《战神斯巴达之子》将于下周登陆 PS4，带来新内容
items.summary: Sony has revealed that God of War Sons of Sparta is coming to PS4 next week, and it's bringing two new modes w

content.v: https://assets-prd.ignimgs.com/2026/02/19/crop-image-project-2-1771515719569.png
Sony has revealed that God of War Sons of Sparta is coming to PS4 next week, and it's bringing two new modes with it.

The unexpected update for this year's action platformer prequel was announced in a PlayStation.Blog post today. In it, Sony confirmed plans to bring Kratos' earliest adventure to the last-gen console starting midnight local time November 16.

It's more than a surprise bonus platform, too, as developer Mega Cat Studios has promised two new modes that will be available on both PS4 and PS5: Hermes Mode and Erebus Mode. The former is described as a "race against the clock" that features speedrunning tools like a split-based timer and a persistent scoreboard. The latter is a one-hit-kill mode that affects both Kratos and his enemies.

Sony and Mega Cat tell God of War Sons of Sparta players that they'll be able to select their mode when starting a new game and selecting a save slot. Game modes can't be changed once selected. Hermes Mode, specifically, is activated only after beating the game once through and after players input the following code: Up, Up, Down, Down, Left, Right, Left, Right, L1, R1, Touchpad. It's unclear if unlocking Erebus Mode has a similar old-school cheat code-esque requirement.

God of War Sons of Sparta takes one of PlayStation's most popular exclusive franchises and scales it down to let players control Kratos at a much, much earlier point in his life in ancient Greece. Shadow-dropped back in February of this year as an experimental chapter of the story for PS5, its story returns to an era fans have longed for with original Kratos actor Terrence 'T.C. Carson back in the booth.

"Every legend has a beginning – before he was a God, before he was a father, Kratos was a young Spartan!" an official story description said. "Experience an untold chapter in Kratos’ journey set during the harsh years of Spartan training alongside his brother Deimos. Through endless trials, their minds, bodies, and hearts have been molded to become Spartan soldiers for whom duty and honor mean everything. After a fellow cadet goes missing, Kratos and Deimos vow to find him and embark on an adventure that will put their training and Spartan spirit to the test."

God of War Sons of Sparta was unable to generate the same level of hype the series' more recent entries have been known for. Despite the surprise of getting a new God of War game without any of the build-up, the prequel side-scroller generally received middling reviews from critics and fans. IGN gave it a 6/10 , calling it "a pretty mediocre Metroidvania" that failed "to meet the high bar set by the titans of the genre."

Franchise creator David Jaffe was less than impressed with God of War Sons of Sparta when it launched. In a video posted at the time, he said a 2.5D God of War game is "the kind of game I've always wanted" but ultimately said it was an experience he did not like and did not recommend. He even went as far as to say, "This is not God of War."

"I wanted to make a video more about what are they thinking, like what the f*** were they thinking?" Jaffe explained. "It's not a bad game by any means, it's fine, it controls decently... but to me the more fascinating part of this is, why is this in existence? I don't understand."

Like it or not, God of War Sons of Sparta offered a stopgap for Sony as it chipped away at the series' next major new entry: God of War Laufey . The PS5-exclusive title is currently set to launch May 20, 2027, following a recent delay . At least the prequel is now available for PS4 users to enjoy while they wait an extra few months.
